intro: A local attention window changes which tokens can influence each other. Edge positions see fewer neighbors, so their weights must be normalized over a smaller set.
task: Compute bidirectional attention within a fixed radius. Use distant-token perturbations to check that excluded positions cannot affect a query’s output.
requirements: queries and keys have matching nonempty shape (S,D); values has shape (S,V) with V>0. radius is an integer in [0,S-1], excluding booleans.
Query i may attend to exactly those keys j with abs(i-j)<=radius. Scale dot products by sqrt(D), apply stable softmax over allowed keys, then combine their values.
Return an (S,V) NumPy array. Radius zero attends only to the token itself; radius S-1 gives full bidirectional attention. There is no causal restriction or padding mask.
Numeric inputs must be real and finite with magnitude at most 1e30, in addition to the bounds above. Leave all inputs unchanged and raise ValueError for invalid inputs.

hints.title: Clip the interval at sequence boundaries
hints.body: Use max(0,i-radius) and min(S,i+radius+1) as slice boundaries.

hints.title: Normalize only the allowed scores
hints.body: Zeroing excluded logits before softmax still gives those positions positive weight.

explanation: Locality can make a distant change invisible to a single layer. Multiple stacked layers can propagate information farther, but this exercise evaluates one attention operation.
The reference processes each local slice directly. The lesson tests the neighborhood and normalization semantics and makes no measured runtime claim.
Ported the upstream bidirectional radius mask to NumPy local slices, avoiding a full score matrix in the reference. Kept the source’s two-sided window rather than silently adding causality.
